title: Prudence (ST II-II.47)
hookLine: right reason in action, the charioteer of the virtues

lines: WISE AS SERPENTS, SIMPLE AS DOVES.
THE ONE THAT STEERS THE REST.
cards: "Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves." Jesus says it in the Douay-Rheims as he sends his disciples out, and it's a strange pairing. Shrewd and innocent at once.
On a given day, managing one or the other can feel like plenty. Back on day three hundred fourteen, prudence was one of the four hinges.
Now Thomas names the virtues one by one, and he begins with the one he thinks steers the rest. Not the flashy one. The one that asks, before you move: what, here, actually needs doing?

teach.b: In everyday English, prudence can sound like carefulness, saving money, never taking a risk. Thomas means something bigger.
Following Aristotle, he calls it right reason applied to action: practical wisdom, seeing in this situation, with these people, what the good thing to do actually is.

Generous, brave and fair people still need to know how to be generous or brave or fair today. The Catechism calls prudence the charioteer of the virtues. The others are the horses; prudence holds the reins.
Thomas breaks it into three steps.
First, take counsel: look at the options, ask, remember what's worked before. Second, judge which option is right. Third, command: actually do it.

teach.h: THE CHIEF ACT IS THE DOING.
teach.b: Thomas says the chief act of prudence is the third one. Not the thinking. The doing.
A person who weighs everything beautifully and never acts isn't prudent. They've stopped halfway. He also warns about fakes.
Cleverness at getting a bad goal is craftiness, not prudence.

teach.h: WISE AS SERPENTS, SIMPLE AS DOVES.
teach.b: And on this account, caution that never moves isn't the virtue either. So the serpent and the dove fit together after all. The serpent's part is clear sight about how things really are.
The dove's part is a clean aim. Prudence is both, ending in an act.

how: Catholic teaching names prudence first among the four cardinal virtues, and Catholics often speak of discernment, seeking counsel and praying before a big decision, as the practice of it.

o: careful saving so you never run short
staying cautious and avoiding every risk
practical wisdom that ends in a good act

p: look at the options and ask
holds the reins of the virtues

s: prudence just means being cautious and avoiding risk
for Thomas it's right reason applied to action, and its chief act is actually doing the right thing.
Thomas says the chief act of prudence is command, the doing
counsel and judgment matter, but someone who never acts has stopped halfway.
for Thomas, cleverness at reaching a bad goal is a kind of prudence
he calls that craftiness, a counterfeit of prudence.

games.q: you've weighed every option and judged which one is right. what does Thomas say prudence asks next?
o: keep weighing until you're completely sure.
act on it: command is the chief act of prudence.
ask someone else to decide for you.
games.why: Thomas names three steps, counsel, judgment and command, and says the chief act is command: doing what you've judged right.

practice: Bring up one decision waiting on you, and walk Thomas's three steps slowly: counsel, weighing the real options and who you could ask; judgment, letting the right one rise to the top; command, naming the very first concrete act and the hour you'll do it.
If you pray, ask for light on the choice.

wordCard.voice: Prudence. Right reason applied to action: taking counsel, judging, and then doing, which Thomas calls its chief act. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: practical wisdom, right reason in action.

carryVoice: Your line: think, then act. Counsel and judgment end in a deed. That's the week.

sources.q: Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves.
